utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Monday, November 16, 2009, and I greet the accused. I also greet the Defence counsel, the eminent members of the OTP, and everyone helping us. Let me first give the floor to our Registrar. He has a number of IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 4D has submitted its objections to Prosecution's list of documents tendered via witness Milan Gorjanc. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1104. 4D has also submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to their list of documents tendered via witness Milan Gorjanc. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1105. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through witness Ivan Beneta. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC1106. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC1107, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC1108. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to ask what the Prosecution thinks about the request for stay -- for addition by the Petkovic Defence. It is proofing -- a proofing document sent to the president of the Community of Herceg-Bosna. It's a report coming from the president of the municipality of Stolac, Mr. Andjelko Markovic, and also written by the -- jointly written by the commander of the Stolac Brigade, Mr. Bozo Pavlovic. This document seems relevant. It is a report on the relations between Croats and Muslims in Stolac, and it was handed over just a few hours ago to the Defence of the Petkovic Defence -- to the Defence. Does the Prosecution have anything to object, as far as adding this exhibit to the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, no, the Prosecution does not object to the addition of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The Trial Chamber adds this document to the 65 ter list. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning [as interpreted], sir. Could you please give us your name, your family name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Bozo Pavlovic. I was born on the 24th of October, 1966, in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation at the moment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a retired colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you already testified in court or is this the first time that you are testifying in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm testifying for the first time here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I will give you some information, but I'm sure Ms. Alaburic has already told you everything about it. You will be answering questions put to you by Ms. Alaburic, who will also show you a number of documents which are in a binder that you have, and the documents will also be displayed on the screen in front of you. After this first phase, the other counsels representing the other accused can also ask questions, if they find it necessary, and then the Prosecutor, who is to your right, Mr. Kruger, will also cross-examine you. I believe he will. The four Judges on the bench can also step in and ask questions on the documents shown to you. Please try to be very specific in your answers. If you don't understand a question, just ask for the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. I'd also like to draw your attention on the fact that whenever a Judge is asking a question that you feel -- whenever you feel that a Judge is asking -- whenever a Judge is asking a question, you can answer to that question as you want. It's not because it's a Judge that you must answer the question in a specific way. Feel free to answer as you wish. The Judge is asking the question to try and maybe get confirmation on something, or to try to shed some light on another item. If you believe that the Judge made a mistake in his question, just say so, and remember that you are completely free when you give your answer. I wanted to tell you all this so that this hearing runs smoothly. Let me also tell you that you have taken the oath, you took the solemn declaration. You are now in the hands of justice, you are a witness of justice. You are not to contact the Defence of General Petkovic for the days to come. I would also invite you not to relate what is happening in this courtroom to anyone, notably the media. If, for example, a reporter came and asked for your feeling on what has been happening, don't say anything, because you are now under oath and you will be under oath until you're done with your testimony. I now greet you again, Ms. Alaburic, and I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to you and my colleagues of the Prosecution, to my Defence colleagues, and you, Mr. Pavlovic, and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pavlovic, we're just briefly going to go through your CV to provide our Judges with information about your education, training, and career. You told us when and where you were born, so now we can go on to your education and hear what schools you've completed. I'm going to read this summary. You can listen to me carefully. Put me right, if I'm wrong. If not, just confirm what I've read out. Now, as far as your education is concerned, you completed a secondary technical school in Stolac, and then specialisation for a technician for air force weapons. Then you completed an officers' school at the level of battalion in Zagreb, and after that the Staff School once again in Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, your career is as follows: You were in the Yugoslav People's Army for three years, and you had the rank of corporal. And at the time, you were a technician in a combat squadron. You were in Zadar for two years, and spent one year in Mostar. In September 1991, you left the JNA, and until April 1992, you had a private firm and took part in the preparations for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In April 1992, you were involved in the Municipal Staff of the HVO of Mostar, and you took part in the liberation of Mostar from the joint forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and the army of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Serbs. On the 1st of July, 1992, you arrived in Stolac as commander of the Municipal Staff of the HVO, and later on that was a forward command post. And you stayed there until the 3rd of July, 1993. Until the 20th of July, 1993, you were involved in the operative section of the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina, and on that same day you were appointed commander of the 3rd HVO Brigade. You remained in that position until the 4th of October, 1993, when a new commander was appointed, the commander of the 3rd Brigade, that is, and you handed over your duties to him ten days later, that is to say, on the 14th of October. In the Staff of the 3rd Brigade of the HVO, you stayed until June 1994, when you went to Zagreb for further education and training. You returned in January 1995 to the Military District of Mostar, and you remained there until February 1996. When you went to work in Sarajevo, you went to the Ministry of Defence of the BH Federation, and you were employed there until March 2001, when you left the ministry and became a private entrepreneur again. You retired in December 2006 with the rank of colonel of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell me, please, Mr. Pavlovic, are the facts that I've read out correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since you were employed in the Ministry of Defence of the BH Federation, I should like to ask you to tell us what was the Army of the Federation composed of at the time when you worked there, when you were in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was composed of two elements, two components; the Croatian Defence Council and the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the first topic we're going to deal with, Mr. Pavlovic, is the situation in Stolac, since your arrival there up until the spring of 1993, so I'd like to ask you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I have a question. You retired in December 2006 as a colonel, colonel of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When your military pension was calculated, could you tell me whether the time you spent in the HVO was taken into account, when you were in the HVO from 1993 to 1994? So could you tell us whether the years you spent with the HVO was actually taken into account when your military pension was computed? Was it taken into account as service with the national forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We didn't get a translation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A "Da," but it wasn't -- it's "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I have an additional question following on from Judge Antonetti's question, who asked you about the time you spent in the HVO in 1993 and 1994. Were your years of service in the HVO recognised, too, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I received double credit for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you mean by "double credit"?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood it when I received my papers, all the time that I spent in the HVO, and later on in the Army of the Federation, was -- well, in the HVO, until the Dayton Accords were signed, it was counted as double years of service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did the same rule apply to the soldiers and officers of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have looked at the law governing that, so we can back that up by the letter of the law. But let's go back to Stolac, 1992. And in order to do that, you can look at the set of documents you have before you, and I'd like to discuss document 4D11483 [as interpreted] as the first document. 1483 is the number, 4D1483. This is a map, Mr. Pavlovic, prepared by our military expert, and it shows the intervention plans of the Yugoslav People's Army in part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, and these plans were compiled in May 1991. Tell us, please, did you have any knowledge of any plans of this kind of the JNA at that time? And we're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this kind of plan, roughly speaking, because from this we can see the axes of advance clearly of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serb forces, and they had the task of breaking through to the Adriatic coast and, in so doing, to cut across the southern reaches of Croatia; that is to say, to cut off Dubrovnik and to occupy parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was in the Mostar area, myself, at the time, and what the Serbian Army did at the time, helped by the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, was -- or, rather, roughly coincides with these axes of attack as drawn in on this map here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "at that time," Mr. Pavlovic, do you mean 1991 or do you mean some other year?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I mean 1991 and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if you recall what was happening in the early spring of 1992, could you tell us whether you have any knowledge and information about the activities of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Serb forces in the area of Kupres, Livno, and the more northerly part, in comparison to where you were?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the area of Kupres, we saw the greatest deployment of Serb forces, and they had strong armoured units, infantry units, and backed up by the air force. They had the assignment of breaking through in the direction of Split from that area, so they were -- the strong forces were deployed in the area of Kupres, and they came there from the direction of Mostar. So we were all able to see them passing by in large columns.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Had the Serbs succeeded in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. This last answer, as recorded, may be wrong. You're recorded as saying that from -- there were large forces in Kupres and, I quote: "... and they came there from the direction of Mostar." Looking at the map, this seems improbable to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they came also from the direction of Mostar. An armoured brigade, in the autumn of 1991, was stopped along the axis of Mostar-Siroki Brijeg in a place called Polak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is understood. The problem is that the sentence reads as if they came from Mostar to Kupres, but what you want to say is from Mostar they also proceeded towards the sea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They also came from Mostar. So they came to Kupres from other directions, but also from Mostar, too. That's what I wanted to say. And the other units launched an attack in the direction of the sea, south of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you're interested in this, perhaps on this map here, the map on our monitors, we could perhaps indicate the movement of JNA forces that the witness is talking about, because the witness did mention certain movements that took place at the end of 1991, and he mentioned some events in 1992, the spring of 1992. So perhaps it wasn't quite clear, but if you want us to clarify all this, then I'm sure the witness can show us what the troop movements were at the end of 1991 and what it was that happened in the spring of 1992; Kupres, Livno, the direction towards Split, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that this map depicts the situation of May 1991, I don't think it's a basis to continue and ask what happens later. I suggest that you go on. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My following question was whether the events in the field, in the early spring of 1992, were exactly as shown on this map concerning the plans of the JNA from 1991. So if you could give us a summary of the events as they happened in spring 1992, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, in spring 1992 the units of the JNA had taken up positions around the town of Mostar. They had taken all hills around the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, if I may interrupt you. I didn't want to go into the details. If you could just state whether the events in spring 1992 corresponded to what's shown here on the map, if that's what you can do by way of summarising.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did correspond, as I've said already.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, who was it at that time, that is, early spring 1992, who was able and willing to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina against such an aggression or offensive actions, whatever way we may choose to call them, from the JNA and the BiH Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was only the Croatian Army that could put up resistance against such forces and the units of the HVO which had organised themselves by that time clandestinely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in that process of organising units, did Muslims who lived in those territories also take part? Did they also participate in the preparations to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In spring, that is, in early 1992, the HVO was being established from units that had been preparing in secret. We prepared for defence and cooperated in the field. We had night guards, and in some areas we were able to stop the advance of these forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you at the time personally participate in some liberation actions?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which actions were those?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I took part in the liberation of the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. As this has been discussed extensively in this courtroom, we will skip that and pass over to Stolac. When did you arrive at Stolac, Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived there on the 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was Stolac liberated at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the town of Stolac was liberated at that moment, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who was it that liberated Stolac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The forces that had liberated Stolac were the forces of the 116th Brigade of the HV, the most -- the strongest element of which was the Stolac Battalion, which was active in the direction of Stolac itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You were not an eye-witness, but you probably heard the accounts of eye-witnesses. Was there any fighting involved in the liberation of Stolac or did the Serbs and the Serb Army simply leave, without resistance, Stolac and the municipality of Stolac too?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: There was fierce fighting for Stolac, the same as for Mostar, at least according to the accounts of my colleagues and later fellow soldiers who were engaged along the direction toward the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Stolac Battalion, at the moment when you arrived at Stolac, what was your position on the 1st of July when you arrived at Stolac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, I was appointed the commander of the Municipal Staff of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean the Municipal Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Municipal HVO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What condition was the Stolac Battalion in? Did they have enough men, were they ready for subsequent combat activity, were they rested?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, the condition of the unit was such that the soldiers had been without relief for quite a while. They were very tired and exhausted by combat. They were holding positions against the Serbs in some areas immediately outside the town of Stolac and other areas in villages to the north-west of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was the commander of the 116th Brigade of the Croatian Army, Colonel Beneta.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you launch any activity with regard to the reorganisation of the Stolac Battalion at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to Stolac, I was tasked with strengthening the positions outside of Stolac, fortify them, and launch active defence. With the forces I had found, I wasn't able to do so. And in co-operation with my superior officer, we started mobilising additional soldiers and enlarging the unit, so that in the following two weeks or so we were able to improve the condition and mobilise as many soldiers as we could equip and arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This additional mobilisation, how was it conducted, by public summons or secret summons, or was it a general mobilisation? Do describe.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to Stolac, there had already been a crisis staff. It was possible to establish it. And within that Crisis Staff, the Mobilisation Department started functioning, because the people who had worked on these jobs before, that is, prior to the Serb aggression, had removed and hidden the registers and the mobilisation documents, so that we had complete insight into the military specialisations of the conscripts. But there was a public mobilisation call, and many soldiers answered the call, even more than we could accept at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since inter-ethnic relations matter greatly in this trial, can you tell us about the ethnic make-up of these people who answered the call?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Almost all able-bodied Croats had already -- or had already been mobilised in the municipality of Stolac, and as a consequence, I dare say that about 90 per cent Muslim conscripts answered that mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What absolute numbers are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there were as many as 400 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly what you did with these people who were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We made a list. We saw what their military specialties were, what they had been trained for in the former army, and some of them were equipped right away, and we started establishing two battalions in accordance with the principle -- a principle which was honoured because the first battalion already had much combat experience, even in attack operations, so that from that first Stolac battalion we took a platoon of about 30 people and added to it another platoon of 30 more people, and those were newly-mobilised soldiers. And that's how we proceeded until we were able to establish two units of the strength of a battalion each.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic make-up of both battalions?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It was roughly on a 50:50 basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the commanding officers; what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We also took into consideration these factors when we were establishing a command structure, but we had an agreement that to start with, we must take into consideration the combat experience of the members of the first battalion. However, in many commanding positions, or positions of chiefs for artillery, or logistics, et cetera, we also included people of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, let's proceed. Tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, in this establishing of a joint army of Croats and Muslims, did you enjoy the support of your superiors or did you do it of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: When I received the order to take over the Municipal Staff of Stolac from my superior officer, I received instructions to, above all, strengthen the defence and include the entire population of the town of Stolac in that defence, irrespective of their ethnicity. And that's the kind of order that I received from Colonel Beneta, too, because he wasn't opposed to including them in the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was your attitude toward these orders? Did you approve of them or did you think that they were wrong, deep down inside?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: If I had considered them wrong, I wouldn't have agreed to carry out these orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the reactions of the Croatian population which by that time had returned to Stolac? Did they praise this effort to establish a joint army or were they basically against it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: There was some disapproval of the decision to include Muslims -- sorry, soldiers of Muslim ethnicity into the units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the probable reasons?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The probable reason was that immediately before leaving Stolac, as a consequence of a strong Serb attack, the Muslim people had not left together with the Croats because the defence of the town of Stolac before that attack had been prepared jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us whether the Muslim population, during the Serbian occupation of Stolac, did they participate with -- or, rather, cooperate with the Serbs in setting up local authorities or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that we had, the Muslim population cooperated with the aggressor, and there was information that their political leadership at the time signed a treaty of loyalty to the Serb Herzegovina. For example, the chief of police and all police services operated as if nothing had happened, and likewise -- or, rather, this applied to all the other services in the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember who the chief of police was at that time in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of police was Mr. Mehmed Dizdar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell me what the position was of the Muslim population with respect to the efforts to set up a joint army of Muslims and Croats. Was there any resistance there on their part?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I experienced at the time was this: I wasn't able to notice that the Muslim population and the Muslim conscripts, which responded to the call-up voluntarily, that they had any misgivings about an HVO army and the Croatian people, and I saw their enthusiasm. They were pleased that they were relieved from the aggressor's pressure, the kind of pressure they felt during the occupation, in fact, and that they felt themselves to be free citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Pavlovic, at that time can you quote a single example of any of the Muslims who had left Stolac wishing to go back to Stolac without being allowed to do so or perhaps being prevented to do so in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary, in fact. We helped as much as we could. We did help the refugees to return. We just did not allow -- in some hamlets along the front-line where our soldiers had been put up, we did not allow them to go back there, and where the civilians could have been exposed to heavy shelling and infantry attacks by the Serb units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this rule that you've just explained to us, did you apply it to the Croats and Muslims alike, or was there any discrimination in that respect?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, this rule held fast for one and all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Tell us, please, Mr. Pavlovic -- yes, we've got the surname spelt properly in the transcript, but does the name Mirsad Mahmutcehajic ring a bell at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was he an inhabitant of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards the establishment of the HVO as a joint army of the Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, when I arrived and during those first few days, I had an opportunity of meeting that particular gentleman, whom I didn't know until then, and he had the opportunity of getting a post in the Logistics Department of our unit. And as far as I understood it, he accepted this offer, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How do you mean that he was offered a post in Logistics?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some of my associates asked me and, in fact, advised me to have this gentleman work in logistics, that it would be a good idea, because according to what they said, he had good connections and he knew all the channels of weapons procurement, and so on and so forth, and that this is something he had engaged in previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did Mr. Mahmutcehajic ever, for the purposes of the HVO in Stolac defence, procure any weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: On two occasions, he asked me to issue him with some permits that he needed to go to Zagreb. He said he had some friends there through whom he could procure what we needed. And at the time, what we needed most was anti-armour rocket defence systems and artillery weapons, and so I gave him permission to do that. However, not once did he bring anything back with him to our Logistics Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information to the effect that Mr. Mahmutcehajic was, in fact, dissatisfied with the way in which the defence of Stolac was organised?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Not until that time, no. However, on one occasion when I and my deputy, Mr. Edin Obradovic, toured the front-lines of our defence, upon our return, on the way back, when talking, he told me that he had had -- that there were some problems among the Muslims, themselves, in Stolac, and that Mr. Mahmutcehajic had caused many of those problems. I asked him to explain what he meant, but he avoided answering me and said that it would be best if the two of us got together, had a meeting. I said, Right, fine, no problem. Where can I find the man? And he told me that he was in Stolac, in a part of town called Uzinovici, and that we could find him down there. I asked him, When? And he said, Whenever you like. So we set off to find him straight away, there and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for a moment. You needn't go into how you found him, but let's take it from the moment you actually found him. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Can I give you an answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived at a feature called Palma in Uzinovici, where we were supposed to find him. We came across a couple of people there, and they told us that he was across the road in the mosque. So we set out towards the mosque, and there were two guards standing in front of the mosque. As we approached, they recognised Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, "Obradovic," that's right. Tell us, this man, Edin Obradovic, your deputy, what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Edin Obradovic was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. So you went up to the guards standing in front of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: They knew Edin from before, I assume, because they referred to him as Mehraba -- they said to him "Mehraba," which is a Muslim greeting. They didn't know me. They probably thought I was his driver, because we didn't have any insignia on us, except on our sleeves, where it said the "HVO/Croatian Defence Council." And they told us that Mr. Mahmutcehajic was inside the mosque. We went into the mosque, said hello to him, but after that he left the mosque straight away, and he started swearing at the two guards. He said to them, Do you know who you just let in? They said they had let Edo in. However, he said, What do you mean, Edo? You've let Pavlovic in. You know who he is? Now, while he was leaving the mosque, Mr. Obradovic and I went 'round the mosque inside, and I found something that surprised me when I walked 'round the inside of it. I counted some crates that were there, and there were over 200 automatic and other types of rifle in the mosque at the time in those boxes, 2 machine-guns, 3 82-millimetre mortars, 6 60-millimetre mortars that were known as the Partisan Mortars, 1 120-millimetre mortar, large quantities of ammunition, grenades, shells, and military equipment of all kinds, and large quantities of food; flour, oil, and other necessities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what did you say to Mr. Mahmutcehajic when he returned to the mosque, Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I first asked him whether that was the weaponry that he had gone to Zagreb to fetch when he asked me to give him permission to do so. He gave me some answers which I can't quite recall now, but I demanded of him at the time that in the course of that day, the 120-millimetre mortar had to be up at the positions and used for the defence of the town of Stolac, because at that time we only had one 120-millimetre mortar, and here we had another one lying idle in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did you negotiate this matter of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him to place it all at our disposal up at the front-line to defend the town. However, he opposed me and said he would distribute this materiel personally as he saw fit. I said that there were rules governing how weapons were to be deployed and distributed and that we knew full well who was able to manage this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there, not to recount your entire conversation with him. Just give us -- tell us what the result was. What agreement did you reach? Did you get any of those weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to take any weapons by force and thereby violate the relations that were improving, the relations between the Croats and the Muslims. They were on the assent. However, I told him that he had to provide us with that 120-millimetre mortar before the day was out, and he agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us, please, all that weaponry, did it remain in the mosque? Do you know anything about what happened to those weapons later on, where they ended up?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons remained in the mosque when we left. However, we later learnt that soon afterwards it was sent to other locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you distribute the weapons or was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pavlovic, going back to that same meeting in the mosque, I'm going to tell you how the meeting was described by a protected witness who appeared in this courtroom. And as he was protected, I can't give you his name, but the pseudonym was CU, and his testimony was recorded on pages 12470 of the transcript and 12471. So here's what that witness said. He said that in July 1992, in the Unuzovic [phoen] Mosque in Stolac, that there was a meeting between Pavlovic, Edin Obradovic, and Mirsad Mahmutcehajic, and that in the courtyard of the mosque there were 27 automatic rifles, and that a platoon had been established, or, rather, a squad, and that the weapons were taken away by Pavlovic and Edin Obradovic. Now, can you tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, whether this description was what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That's just not correct. There were just two armed guards standing in front of the mosque, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now let's look at the organisational changes that took place in Stolac. Last week in this courtroom, we had General Beneta, who told us that in mid-July he had left Stolac. Now, tell us, is that what happened? Did General Beneta really leave Stolac in mid-July 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was Colonel Beneta at the time, and he handed over the positions and left Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, at that time, the Municipal Staff of the HVO of Stolac, did it undergo any reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Municipal Staff of Stolac, at that time, that is to say, when the 116th Brigade left, Group 2, TG-2, well, two battalions had already been established, and he had units under the battalion, and they managed to stabilise the front-line and make the town safer, to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did these two battalions of the HVO -- or, rather, tell us, what brigade were the two Stolac battalions a part of?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The two Stolac battalions, once the 116th Brigade had left, were placed under the command of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the battalions have their respective commanders?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You were not a battalion commander, were you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, who was it that co-ordinated the activities of these two battalions in the Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: When they were taken out of the 116th Brigade and became part of the 1st HVO Brigade, the command post was transformed into a forward command post, and its role was to co-ordinate the units in the territory of the Stolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was it possible for the commander of the 1st HVO Brigade to communicate directly with the commanders of the Stolac battalions?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there instances when the brigade commander directly -- was in direct communication with the battalion commanders?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pavlovic -- we're still speaking about the month of July. Can you tell us what the Serbs were doing at the time? Had they retreated completely? Had they given up Stolac? Was there peace prevailing in Stolac, without any fighting, or was the situation different?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time after my arrival, the Serbs were also involved in a complete reorganisation, they fortified their positions, but they were also daily engaging in active defence. That is, they were intensively shelling our positions, the town itself and its surroundings. They also had reconnaissance missions, and they were preparing for a counter-attack on our units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did that counter-attack actually come about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe -- or, rather, tell us, then, the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe that attack for the Bench to get an impression of the scope of the attack? Was it merely a skirmish or was it more serious than that, with wounded and killed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I dare say that the attack was -- possibly was more intensive than our attack when we pierced through Serb positions and took positions around Mostar and the town of Stolac. On that day, some 4.000 to 4.500 enemy shells were fired at us. We were attacked from several directions. Along one direction, they were even able to pierce our defence lines, whereas elsewhere we managed to defend ourselves. There were three attacks of theirs. The first was launched at 6.00 a.m. It was the fiercest. The second was around 10.00, or 9.30 to be precise, which was almost as strong as the previous one at 6.00 a.m. And the third attack followed at 2.00 p.m. It was rather weaker. I have to point out that on that day, the Serb Air Force was also active. There were many casualties on both sides. We had three killed soldiers. It was -- the names were Papac, Zukanovic, and Obradovic. There was about a dozen wounded, more or less seriously wounded, and the Serb forces had much greater casualties, greater losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us see what a document says about the losses on the Serb side. Could we please go into private session, because the document I'm about to show is protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, please take a look at the following document, 2D1295. It's an order. Did you have an opportunity to see this order during the proofing?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what kind of order is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It's a defence order signed by General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Has this order anything to do with Operation Bura?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and it shows that -- it shows which units were tasked with fortifying existing positions in Operation Bura and which units are tasked with preventing the enemy from launching a counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does it follow from this document that the defence was -- the defence concept was that of a joint defence by the HVO and the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, in your evidence so far, you mentioned that when you came to Stolac on the 1st of July, 1992, there was a crisis staff. Can you tell us who the president of the Crisis Staff was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Crisis Staff was Mr. Zeljko Raguz.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What had been his position before the war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the Stolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the ethnic make-up of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it consisted of 50:50 Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I would now like to quickly go through some documents I consider important for the period when you were active in the Stolac municipality and which speak about the co-operation between Croats and Muslims in defence. Take a look at document P314, please. This is your document or the document by which you are appointed -- by which you appoint the commander and deputy commander of the 2nd Battalion. Could you read out their names, please, and their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muharem Dizdar is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to correct the name. The name is Muharem Dizdar. Tell us about the ethnicity of his deputy, Ilija Markovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the following document, 4D914. This is one of your reports from July 1992, and here, at the third paragraph, it is stated that the command -- the staff command works intensively on the establishment of mixed Croatian-Muslim units. Is this what you described as a creation of a joint Croat-Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On page 3, that is, toward the very end of the document, it reads that about 90 per cent of the Muslims responded to the mobilisation. Is this what you mentioned when the Muslims answered the call-up in great numbers?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at document 4D908, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I have something to ask. In the last document, 4D914, this is a report that you wrote, and you say four joint companies were set up and one purely Muslim company was also set up. While I was reading this, I was wondering why you didn't also set up a purely Croat company. Was there a reason behind this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll explain this document to you. I told you at the beginning that at that time, there was a purely Croatian battalion, the Stolac Battalion, and that that was the basis for the establishment of two battalions later on. Now, we took in all those who had their own weapons, and we armed those others who did not. At that point in time, the village of Prenj, within the Stolac municipality, had -- that is to say, illegally had, during the Serb occupation, a company. This company had been illegally formed, and that company placed itself at our disposal during the mobilisation period. The date here is the 12th of July, and at that time we still hadn't established those two battalions. That is why it was still purely Muslim. But over the next few days, it became a mixed battalion, together with the Croats. So after that, we no longer had any ethnically pure units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the next document, which is 4D908, and this is a letter from the Bregava commander, Bajro Pizovic. Tell us what army this is.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It's the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, from this document, we can see that a BH Army commander is addressing the command of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade of the HVO and is requesting an area of responsibility and a location in which to put up his unit. Have I interpreted this document correctly? Is that what it's about? Is it, indeed, a request sent to an HVO brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that was quite normal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "quite normal," do you mean that areas of responsibility were being ascribed and that you were putting up a joint defence against the Serbs? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next document is 4D932, and here Mr. Mahmutcehajic is addressing Mr. Nedjeljko Obradovic. Tell us, what function did this man Obradovic have?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade of the HVO Brigade called the Knez Domagoj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Once you read the first passage of this very short letter, what is expected here is that the HVO commander should introduce the Bregava Brigade to strengthen the defence abilities of the town of Stolac. Now, based on your experience and this document, is that proof of co-operation between the two armies or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is precisely proof and evidence of co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D624, and this is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll look at the following document after the break. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The court is back in session. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, we're going to cut short some documents from the bundle because time is flying, so we're going to skip to the next document. We're going to look at 4D1521, 1521. We have a small mistake in the date here, and it's not "December," but it's "January," and we can see that from the contents of the document. Can you please tell us -- Mr. Pavlovic, at the bottom of the page we can see a stamp. Can you please tell us what this stamp means?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is a receipt stamp of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which unit; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It's the Bregava Brigade in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So that means that the brigade received the document from the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can you please tell us what the orders are, then, for the Bregava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It is being commanded or ordered to take up its assigned positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document, 4D1553. It's the order by the chief of the Main Staff of January 1993, and it says: "In connection with a conference in Geneva and due to the potential enemy activities on the Stolac front, I hereby issue the following:" Mr. Pavlovic, can you please tell us, who was the enemy at the Stolac front at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In item 1 of this order, the forming of a unit of 70 men is being referred to. Did that unit come to the Stolac area in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was its assignment?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It was a reserve force which we could deploy along a certain axis.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. The next document, 4D1026. It's a combat report from the Bregava Brigade commander, Mr. Bajro Pizovic, and in the middle section of the document he says: "Our forces responded forcefully to the Chetnik attack, together with the HVO forces." Can you please tell us, in this document, are the HVO and the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army at that point in time, in February 1993, fighting together or holding positions against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they're holding positions jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're going to skip the next document, and we're now going to look at 4D1048. Judging by the preamble to this order from February 1993, who is the enemy at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, the chief of the Main Staff is ordering that the units of the B and H Army be informed about the same danger so that they could also reinforce their defence lines. Can you please tell us whether this was passed on to the B and H Army or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And does it represent an agreement between the two forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at 4D478. This document actually consists of two documents. It's a request Bajro Pizovic, the commander of the Bregava Brigade, is sending to the operative zone of the HVO, requesting artillery support. And in response to that request -- just one second. I have an instruction to correct something in the transcript, so I just need to understand what it's about. Very well. It's all right. And then we have the response from Mr. Lasic about long-range artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether -- oh, yes, I see. Excuse me, I was mistaken about the number of the document because -- but it seems to be the one. You are on 478, and you skipped 1048; right? No, you had it. I'm sorry, I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did skip one. I'm going to skip some documents because I had a more or less optimistic option in terms of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this response by Miljenko Lasic speaks about long-term artillery. Can you please explain this reply?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Long-range artillery was entrusted to the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operations Zone, and all units under the command of the commander of that zone had the right to request artillery support if they needed such support. So the Bregava Brigade, too, exercised its right, and you could use your own artillery for targets that were in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, in terms of this long-range artillery, were you and your units and the Bregava Brigade in the same position, in terms of using this option?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the units were in the same position, as far as making a request of this type was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to skip a document again, and can we please look at document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Colonel, we're looking at these two documents, and I'm trying to understand. On the 6th of February, the commander of the Bregava Brigade asked for support, for artillery support, but he made the request to the HVO. And on the 7th of July [as interpreted], he got an answer from the HVO. Basically, he got an agreement from the HVO. Now, based on the examination of these two documents, because you were on the ground and you know better than anyone what was happening, should we conclude that in February 1993, there was, between the HVO and the ABiH, co-ordination in the fight -- in the military fight against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from what I understood you to say, you said that the reply was sent to the 7th of July, if the interpretation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7th of February. I said "7th of February," sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see from this document that co-operation at the time was good, because at the time units of the Croatian Defence Council and the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army were keeping control in the area of responsibility side by side and were defending the line, the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to skip a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 4D476. It's a report by the security organs of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army 4th Corps, and in the conclusion, under line 7, it says that: "Relations between the army and the HVO at Rotimlje are very good." Mr. Pavlovic, can you please tell us, are you able to confirm or deny this assertion?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This assertion is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And is Rotimlje in the Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It belongs to the Stolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were your units in charge of defence of that area in Rotimlje?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not in charge of the Rotimlje defence, but I had the opportunity to come to Rotimlje very often at that time, because that's where my house is and I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were your parents in Rotimlje at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the time, but I would very often drive there to stop by and check my house, my property, to visit my neighbours and my relatives, so that I could see for myself that the situation at Rotimlje was without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the last document from this segment. It's 4D475. We've already seen this document several times in the courtroom. It's a request for active defence, and it was issued by the commander of the Operative Zone Southern Herzegovina, and it was issued on the 23rd of February, 1993. And in item 3, they're talking about Bregava line of defence. Mr. Pavlovic, can you please tell us whether that was actually the line held by the Bregava Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Rudina area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am being told to correct page 37, line 4, and that we're talking about the order, not a request. So it's an order, not a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now we can move to another topic about relations between Muslims and Croats in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the fact that they are becoming more complex at this time. Let's look at the documents to try to see how the situation became more complex and more complicated in the relationship between Croats and Muslims. Now let's look at 4D929, please, 929. This is a report by Mehmed Dizdar from early January 1993. Mr. Pavlovic, can you please tell us if you had the opportunity to read this document while you were preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to read the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to summarise the contents. I'm not going to read the entire document. It's quite a long one. But it's clear from the document that the following persons are trying to contact policemen of Muslim ethnicity and persuade them to join the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army and to leave the police force which was actually a joint police force with the Croats. Those people are: Mehmed Dizdar, who wrote the document, followed by Mirsad Mahmutcehajic, Esad Suta, Alija Rizanbegovic [phoen], and members of the Crisis Staff. Mr. Pavlovic, can you please tell us if at the time you knew that persons who occupied some party posts or military positions were trying to exert influence on Muslims in the police who wished to co-operate with Croats?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who was the main source of this information?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, they were the people who actually they were trying to influence. They were the policemen from the Stolac police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were these Muslim policemen?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document, 4D1603, 1603. What I would like to know from you, Mr. Pavlovic -- we're just going to look at the cover page of this document, and we had the opportunity to analyse this document before in the courtroom. Can you just interpret this stamp at the bottom on this page?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the receipt stamp?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the receipt stamp by the Bregava Brigade in Stolac, indicating that the document was received.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is all I wanted to know from this document. Can we look at the next document, 4D1027. This is a document by the Security Service of the HVO 1st Brigade which says that the Command of the Bregava Brigade, without any kind of announcement, came to Gubavica, set up a check-point in Pijesci, and that they were planning to go to Bivolje Brdo Hill. Can you please tell us whether the fact that Bregava came to these locations was an act that resulted of their own will or was it a consequence of some command from the HQ?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, they came of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if at the time you were aware of the fact that they had come to this location on their own ?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And how did you feel about this unannounced arrival at this particular location, you and the HVO units in that area? Was that something normal?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was a form of provocation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at the next document, 4D428. What I would like to look at with you here, Mr. Pavlovic, is actually two things. This is a report of the 4th Corps Command, the Section for Morale, Information, Political Activity and Religious Affairs, and it says: "Deterioration of the relations in the region of the municipality of Konjic had some influence on the soldiers' morale." The Defence often tried to prove in this courtroom that we were unable to understand the events in Mostar unless we knew what happened in the area of Jablanica and Konjic, and that this was all interconnected and influenced the relationship, the atmosphere, and the understanding among the sides, so can you please give us an insight about the situation and tell us whether this interconnectedness actually reflected the situation that prevailed at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a closely-connected area, and any event that would have any kind of influence, in terms of the deterioration of relations between the HVO and the B and H Army or, rather, Croats and Muslims, would powerfully reflect on all the units in that area, and of course would also be felt among the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you know, can you please tell us whether the Konjic, Jablanica, and Mostar area was part of a single corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, and was it part of one operations zone? Was it organised in that way?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now can we look at this second part of the document, where it says that: "Another problem is also the opinion among some of the soldiers who think that the war is over with the signing of the Vance-Owen Plan, so that it would be necessary to implement a number of measures in order to activate the combat morale among that part of the soldiers." Can you, as a soldier, explain what these measures would be to activate the combat morale among a part of the fighters?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were actions of low intensity, that is to say, creating incidents, storming certain areas without any announcement. It would also include opening fire without permission and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at P1809, which is the next document, please, 1809. It's an order from the Command of the Bregava Brigade, dated the 5th of April, 1993, and from this document we can see that the command is located in the village of Gubavica. Now, was the command indeed put up there with the HVO's agreement or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Bregava Brigade Command was accommodated in South Camp, whereas the forward command post and the command post of the unit which held the line was in the village of Rotimlje, and I think the hamlet itself was called Kajtezovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What you've just told us now, is that how things should have been in agreement with the HVO or is that how things were?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It's the area of responsibility assigned to them in agreement with the HVO, but in reality the situation was that off their own bat, they reached the Gubavica area and took control of the barracks of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, this document is ordering stepped-up combat readiness in all units of the brigade. Did you know about this increase in combat readiness for the Bregava Brigade units?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How could you know that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, through intelligence work, the intelligence we gathered in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there any large movements in the area when combat readiness was raised?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. They would assume their positions, and then it would be normal that the troops would be deployed in the area so that they could perform the tasks assigned them by their superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at 4D568, the next document, please, 4D568, and this, in our opinion, is a very important document from the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces, the Security Section. And it says in the last part of the document that it was realistic to expect relations to come to a head and even to expect a confrontation between the BH Army and the HVO. And now I quote the last sentence in that passage. It reads as follows: "It is very important to prepare ourselves for such a situation and to inactivate the Muslims who are in the HVO and to exercise influence on them to move over from the HVO to the Army of the BH." Now, Mr. Pavlovic, did you in the HVO at the time know about this kind of policy pursued by the BH Army with respect to the Muslim soldiers, the Muslim component in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D1715, and this is a special report on the Bregava Brigade which, in December 1993, was set up in the Security Section of the BH Army. It's a special piece of information, and we're interested in something it says on the last page of the document, that is to say, page 3 of the Croatian version and I assume it's the last page of the English version. So the last page, third paragraph from the bottom, and it says here as follows, that: "The HVO, on the 22nd of April, 1993, attacked the Command of the Bregava Brigade which, with the brigade police, was moving towards Stolac, so that in the area of Osanici it encountered an ambush and all 20 members of the command, except Smajo Cerkez, were arrested, captured, and taken to the camp, just like other members of the Bregava Brigade had previously been captured and taken away." Now, do you know what the situation was like in Osanici, and the fact that these people were captured and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this information is partially correct, because it wasn't the fact that 20 people were captured, but just 3, 3 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of those three?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pizovic, Mr. Sijercic, and Mr. Zujo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's repeat those surnames so that we don't have to correct the transcript later on. Bajro Pizovic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dzemil Sijercic and Meho Zujo?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll deal with that later on, we'll correct the transcript. But, anyway, in that action of uncovering and capturing members of the Bregava Brigade, did your soldiers take part in that operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who else took part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I'm impressed by the fact that you know these names after all this time. Have you had those present in your memory all the time, or has your memory been refreshed recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that one of them is my next-door neighbour, in fact. I know the men. I can't forget them. I know the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, the first name we mentioned, we've seen it -- come across it in many documents. He was commander of the Bregava Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So who else took part in this action of uncovering these people and capturing them, in addition to your men?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian police took part and the military police did, a military police platoon, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know who did the actual capturing, who actually captured the men?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian police captured them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you something about the paragraph above, which describes how certain members of the BH Army went off in various directions, and it says that part of the men, about 15 of them, pulled out towards Blagaj and another part towards Sevac Njive, Pocitelj and Domanovici, and operated independently, and then on the 13th of July, 1993, during a BH Army action on the Dubrava Plateau, they joined up with the 42nd Mountain Brigade of the BH Army. Tell me now, please, Mr. Pavlovic, do you happen to know what this action on the 13th of July was all about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt from my colleagues what this was about, but at the time I, myself, was far away from that area, so I can't tell you anything with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And according to what your colleagues told you, did the BH Army actually engage in action on the Dubrava Plateau on that particular day, the 13th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, during the night between the 12th and 13th of July, 1993, they used a number of groups and stormed the HVO from behind, from different directions. And with respect to the units you just mentioned, they went into action and attacked from the rear, from the back, the HVO units, and there were quite a lot of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that the HVO at that time was preparing some liberation operations in that area south of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know what that operational action was called?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was called "Operation South."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know about that operation from your colleagues in the operations zone, the people you worked with?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was superficial information. I didn't take part in all that, so I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you something with respect to General Petkovic, who was chief of the Main Staff at the time. Did you have any information about General Petkovic taking part in the planning of that operation in any way and executing it, or in executing supervision over the operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mr. Pavlovic, I'm now going to ask you to focus on a rule that a witness with the pseudonym CR spoke about and referred to, and that was on page 11941 of the transcript. He said that in the army, there was a general rule that was followed whereby the soldier of one unit, when entering the zone of another unit, was supposed to report and announce himself. Now, to the best of your knowledge, does such a regulation exist?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that rule does exist, and I always respected it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's take a look at a few documents on that subject to see how the Bregava Brigade respected that rule. And the first of those documents is P1736, which is an order by the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, dated the 27th of March, 1993, and I'd like us to look at item 2, where it says that: "Other units are forbidden to enter the areas of responsibility, other than their own, without the consent of the commander of that unit and his superior command." Tell me now, please, Mr. Pavlovic, is that precisely the rule we've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I see here that this order was sent to the commander of an operative zone, which would mean that it is a rule that holds true for the units of the same army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D474. And it's an order, once again, from the commander of your operative zone, with the same contents expressed in item 2. Now, tell me, did this order reach you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but through the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now let's look at the next document, which is 5D3046. This is one of your documents, and in the introduction you say the same thing, that the objective was to prevent incidents from breaking out in the Operative Zone of Stolac. Could you expound on that? Could you explain the document to us in a few words?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best. This is an agreement that was reached between the 1st Herzegovina Brigade of the HVO and the Bregava Brigade to the effect that all movement from the area of responsibility should be announced in advance, and that there would be no problems for those activities to take place if they were announced. That means that if one of my soldiers were to leave his position and go into hiding in the area of responsibility controlled by the Bregava Brigade, for example, then it is my duty to send in a request to the commander of the Bregava Brigade, and it is his duty, in turn, on the basis of that request from me, to deploy his military policemen to capture the soldier and send him to a contact point, escort him to a contact point. Now, if a soldier of the Bregava Brigade were to leave his positions, then he sends me -- his commander sends me a request to that effect, then our military police takes him into custody and escorts him to a point of contact, so that there should be no problems among the and between the zones, the areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at the next two documents. P1913 is a request from the Command of the 1st Brigade with respect to entering an area of responsibility without written permission. And the second document is P1900. That's an order with roughly the same contents. What we're interested in here is the following: Mr. Pavlovic, did you know about these requests and orders from the commander of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC
